paragraphs: Controlling generated text involves two related tasks: writing new text with a requested attribute, and changing an existing passage just enough to give it that attribute. The paper brings these tasks into one causal framework. Its motivation is that ordinary conditional models can reproduce misleading associations in training data, including gender stereotypes, while trying to satisfy the requested control.

The framework represents generation using a structural causal model. Producing new text becomes an intervention: setting an attribute and considering the resulting text. Editing becomes a counterfactual question: how would this particular text differ if its attribute changed? This distinction gives the two tasks a shared foundation while preserving the special requirement that editing remain tied to an existing passage.

The authors apply the approach when confounding factors responsible for spurious correlations are observed for only a small portion of the data. Their experiments report significantly better control accuracy and lower bias than earlier conditional models. These findings support using causal reasoning to improve both attribute control and resistance to unwanted associations in the studied setting.
neurips-2021-a-causal-lens-for-controlla.tldr: A unified causal framework improves text attribute control and reduces generation bias in experiments with partially observed confounders.

paragraphs: Q-learning uses estimated action values to guide decisions, but these estimates can become systematically too optimistic. Combining several value estimators can help, although the resulting bias depends strongly on how many estimators contribute to the learning target. A fixed choice is difficult to get right because approximation errors change as learning progresses.

The paper derives upper and lower bounds on estimation bias and uses them to motivate adjusting the ensemble size during training. AdaEQ first characterizes approximation error and then treats that information as feedback for changing the ensemble. Drawing on Model Identification Adaptive Control, the method aims to keep bias close to zero as the underlying errors evolve.

This makes ensemble size an actively controlled part of learning rather than a single setting chosen in advance. Experiments on the MuJoCo benchmark show that AdaEQ can improve learning performance over existing methods. The contribution connects a theoretical account of bias with a practical feedback mechanism; the stated goal is nearly unbiased estimation, rather than an unconditional claim that all estimation error disappears.
neurips-2021-adaptive-ensemble-q-learnin.tldr: AdaEQ adjusts the number of value estimators using error feedback to reduce changing estimation bias during Q-learning.

paragraphs: Making a Bayesian neural network infinitely wide can simplify its analysis, but the resulting description has fixed representations. Finite networks can adapt their internal features to the task, which previous work suggests may sometimes give them an advantage. This paper studies how that adaptation first appears when a network is wide but still finite.

The analysis focuses on average feature kernels, which describe relationships induced by hidden representations. The authors argue that the leading corrections caused by finite width have a largely universal form for Bayesian networks with a linear readout and Gaussian likelihood. These assumptions define the scope of the claim, and the focus on leading corrections concerns the first departures from infinite-width behavior.

The paper explicitly illustrates the argument in deep linear fully connected networks, deep linear convolutional networks, and networks with one nonlinear hidden layer. Across these tractable cases, the results begin to explain how task information shapes hidden features. The contribution is a theoretical account of representation adaptation, rather than a demonstration that finite networks always outperform infinite ones.
neurips-2021-asymptotics-of-representati.tldr: The paper characterizes leading finite-width changes in Bayesian network representations under linear-readout and Gaussian-likelihood assumptions.

paragraphs: An object represented as a 3D point cloud can appear in many orientations, even though its meaningful parts remain the same. This paper learns to decompose such objects into capsules while also learning a consistent reference pose. Training uses pairs of randomly rotated objects, so the supervision comes from transformations of the data itself.

The architecture uses permutation-equivariant attention, allowing its decomposition to respect changes in the ordering of input points. It combines attention masks into semantic keypoints and uses those keypoints to supervise capsule behavior under rotation. The aim is to preserve relevant part identity while allowing pose-related quantities to transform appropriately, producing a semantically consistent decomposition.

Learning this decomposition also enables canonicalization: expressing objects in an object-centered reference frame that supports reasoning about their structure. The method needs neither classification labels nor manually aligned training examples. The authors report performance beyond the state of the art on point-cloud reconstruction, canonicalization, and unsupervised classification, showing that the learned representation is useful across these evaluated tasks.
neurips-2021-canonical-capsules-self-sup.tldr: Canonical Capsules learns consistent object parts and reference poses from randomly rotated point clouds without labels or manual alignment.

paragraphs: In a causal bandit problem, an action changes a variable in a causal system, and the learner seeks interventions that yield good rewards. Relationships between variables can provide useful structure for learning. Earlier approaches discussed in the paper assume that the learner already knows the entire causal graph, an assumption the authors seek to remove.

The paper develops algorithms that operate without advance knowledge of that graph. They cover causal trees, causal forests, and a broader class of causal graphs. Under conditions described as mild, their regret guarantees substantially improve on those of standard multi-armed bandit algorithms. Regret measures the reward lost through learning and choosing actions instead of consistently selecting an optimal action.

The authors also prove that their conditions are necessary for the stated advantage: without them, one cannot improve over standard bandit algorithms. Together, the positive and negative results explain when causal structure can help even though it is initially unknown. The benefit is conditional on properties of the problem, rather than following merely from calling the actions causal interventions.
neurips-2021-causal-bandits-with-unknown.tldr: Causal bandit algorithms can outperform standard bandit guarantees without knowing the graph, under conditions also shown to be necessary.

paragraphs: The paper studies causal effects when a treatment has internal structure, such as a graph, image, or piece of text. Its target is the conditional average treatment effect: how an average causal effect varies with the conditions being considered. This extends the estimation problem beyond treatments represented by a simple category or numerical dose.

Under a weak condition on the effect, the authors propose a generalized Robinson decomposition. The decomposition separates the causal quantity of interest from other parts of the learning problem, reducing bias introduced by regularization. It also allows arbitrary learning models to be plugged into the framework, making the estimation strategy compatible with different ways of representing structured inputs.

Under mild assumptions, the method has a quasi-oracle convergence guarantee, providing theoretical support for its estimation behavior. Experiments involving small-world graphs and molecular graphs show better treatment-effect estimation than prior work. The contribution combines flexibility in the models used for learning with an explicit focus on protecting the causal target from regularization bias.
neurips-2021-causal-effect-inference-for.tldr: A generalized Robinson decomposition enables flexible causal-effect estimation for structured treatments while reducing regularization bias.

paragraphs: Deep metric learning seeks representations that transfer to test distributions and classes that were unknown during training. Yet a common evaluation uses just one randomly assigned split between training and test classes. The paper argues that this gives too narrow a picture of generalization because deployment can involve shifts with very different levels of difficulty.

The authors introduce ooDML, a benchmark built from systematically constructed training and test splits of increasing difficulty. This creates a broader range of distribution shifts on which to compare methods. The resulting evaluation asks both how well a method transfers and how its performance changes as the mismatch between training and testing becomes more demanding.

Their empirical analysis finds that generalization tends to deteriorate as difficulty rises, while some methods preserve performance better than others. They also propose few-shot metric learning as an efficient response to unknown test shifts and report consistent improvements on ooDML. The findings make robustness across different shifts a central comparison, rather than relying on a single split's result.
neurips-2021-characterizing-generalizati.tldr: ooDML evaluates metric learning across increasingly difficult distribution shifts and finds that few-shot learning consistently improves generalization.

paragraphs: This paper applies Transformer attention to learning operators associated with partial differential equations. It also examines why attention works in this setting, using operator approximation theory in Hilbert spaces. A central question is whether the familiar softmax normalization is essential to the approximation ability of the attention mechanism.

The analysis shows that softmax is sufficient but not necessary. Without it, a linearized Transformer variant has layer-wise approximation capacity comparable to a Petrov-Galerkin projection, with an estimate independent of sequence length. The authors also introduce a layer-normalization scheme inspired by that projection. It lets scaling information propagate through attention layers, helping with operator-learning tasks involving unnormalized data.

The resulting Galerkin Transformer is evaluated on the viscous Burgers equation, interface Darcy flow, and an inverse problem for identifying interface coefficients. The paper reports significant improvements in training cost and evaluation accuracy relative to softmax-normalized counterparts. These results connect an attention design choice to an approximation-theoretic explanation and practical gains in the tested operator-learning problems.
neurips-2021-choose-a-transformer-fourie.tldr: Galerkin Transformer uses attention without softmax and a projection-inspired normalization to improve the tested PDE operator-learning tasks.

paragraphs: Time-series imputation fills gaps in sequences of measurements. A probabilistic approach describes possible missing values rather than committing only to one answer. CSDI brings score-based diffusion modeling to this task, conditioning its predictions on the values that are actually observed so that available measurements guide how the gaps are filled.

The key design choice is to train the conditional diffusion model explicitly for imputation. This lets it exploit correlations among observed values, connecting the information already present in a sequence to the values that need reconstruction. The method therefore adapts diffusion modeling to the particular information pattern of missing-data problems.

On healthcare and environmental data, the authors report improvements of 40–65% over existing probabilistic imputation methods on commonly used performance metrics. For deterministic imputation, they report error reductions of 5–20% relative to state-of-the-art deterministic methods. CSDI also supports interpolation and probabilistic forecasting, with results competitive with existing baselines. These findings show usefulness across several related time-series tasks while keeping the largest reported gains specific to imputation.
neurips-2021-csdi-conditional-score-base.tldr: CSDI trains diffusion models specifically to fill time-series gaps using observed values, improving probabilistic and deterministic imputation in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper develops a multi-armed bandit algorithm with differential privacy in the shuffle model. A bandit learner repeatedly chooses among actions while learning which ones provide higher rewards. The theoretical question is how much reward it must lose during that learning process when it also has to satisfy a specified privacy guarantee.

The authors provide two regret bounds. One depends on the reward gaps between suboptimal actions and the best action, with a sum of log T divided by each positive gap. The other avoids dependence on those gaps and has a leading term proportional to the square root of kT log T. Here, k counts actions and T counts rounds.

Both bounds add a privacy term proportional to k times the square root of log(1/delta), times log T, divided by epsilon. This makes the privacy contribution explicit alongside the usual learning contribution. The upper bound nearly matches the best known centralized-model regret and substantially improves on the best known local-model algorithm, establishing a strong theoretical tradeoff for the shuffle setting.
neurips-2021-differentially-private-mult.tldr: A private bandit algorithm in the shuffle model achieves regret bounds close to centralized guarantees and better than known local-model guarantees.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation often learns a representation whose overall distribution looks the same in source and target domains. However, making these distributions match does not by itself produce the best representation for classification. This paper examines the transformation used to create that representation and asks whether the same transformation should be applied in every domain.

The authors argue that when source and target data supports overlap, a domain-independent map may be unsuitable for adaptation through invariant features. Their proposed technique gives the transformation both the input features and information about the domain. This allows the mapping into the latent representation to depend on the context in which an input occurs.

The model also uses the property that causal mechanisms change minimally across domains to preserve information relevant to the prediction target. The aim is to achieve useful invariance without discarding valuable classification information. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the method's effectiveness, supporting the value of domain-aware transformations in the settings studied.
neurips-2021-domain-adaptation-with-inva.tldr: Domain-aware representation mappings can preserve predictive information while addressing shortcomings of fixed invariant-feature transformations.

paragraphs: Online learning must sometimes cope with an environment that changes during the sequence of decisions. Adaptive regret evaluates performance over intervals, using the largest static regret on any interval. This exposes periods of poor adaptation that a single comparison over the entire sequence might obscure, making it a useful objective for changing environments.

Earlier adaptive-regret algorithms described in the paper handle particular types of convex functions and require prior parameter knowledge. The proposed algorithm combines two ideas: maintaining multiple learning rates, as in MetaGrad, and using sleeping experts to respond to changes over time. Together, these mechanisms address uncertainty about both the functions and the environment.

The resulting method adapts automatically to convex, exponentially concave, or strongly convex functions, as well as to stationary or changing conditions. It also permits the function type to change between rounds. The paper presents this as the first universal algorithm for minimizing adaptive regret of convex functions, bringing function-class adaptation and adaptation over time into a shared approach.
neurips-2021-dual-adaptivity-a-universal.tldr: Combining multiple learning rates with sleeping experts yields an online algorithm that adapts to both changing environments and different convex function types.

paragraphs: Estimating a person's 3D pose from a wearable camera requires connecting visual evidence to plausible body motion. This paper combines kinematic pose prediction, dynamics modeling, and information about nearby objects. Its central idea is to let a physics-based model help train the model that proposes poses, linking the two components through direct feedback.

At each time step, the kinematic model predicts a target pose from the video and current simulation state. A previously learned dynamics model then tries to reproduce that pose inside a physics simulator. The difference between the requested pose and the pose actually produced becomes a signal for improving the kinematic model.

The method also incorporates objects' six-degree-of-freedom poses, describing their positions and orientations. This supplies context for interactions with objects such as chairs and boxes. The authors demonstrate physically plausible human-object interaction estimates using a single wearable camera and evaluate the approach in both laboratory and real-world settings. The contribution is the tightly integrated training process that connects appearance, motion, and object context.
neurips-2021-dynamics-regulated-kinemati.tldr: Physics-simulation feedback trains a video-based pose predictor to estimate plausible human-object interactions from a wearable camera.

paragraphs: Neuroimaging regression problems can involve structure across both space and time, in the quantities being estimated and in measurement noise. Ignoring temporal relationships loses part of that structure, while modeling them can make inference expensive. This paper develops a hierarchical Bayesian framework intended to retain those relationships while making inference more efficient.

The framework represents the covariance of model parameters and noise using Kronecker products, giving the spatial and temporal structure an organized mathematical form. Inference uses majorization-minimization optimization with guaranteed convergence properties. The algorithms further exploit the Riemannian geometry of temporal autocovariance matrices, using their mathematical structure to guide efficient updates.

For stationary dynamics represented by Toeplitz matrices, the authors use circulant embeddings. They prove convex bounding properties and derive the corresponding update rules, connecting the computational procedure to its theoretical foundations. Evaluations on synthetic data and real M/EEG measurements show improved performance. The result is a structured approach to inference that addresses temporal dependence in both the signal parameters and the noise.
neurips-2021-efficient-hierarchical-baye.tldr: A structured Bayesian framework models spatial and temporal dependencies in signals and noise while enabling efficient inference with convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers can spend substantial computation and memory processing image patches that contribute little useful information. IA-RED² addresses this redundancy by learning to drop uncorrelated patches dynamically. The selection module is designed to be interpretable, making the reduction in processing connected to visible evidence about which parts of an input matter.

The framework also applies this idea hierarchically. Tokens are removed gradually at different processing stages, reducing the amount of computation carried forward. This makes selection part of the model's ongoing processing rather than a single decision made before the image or video has been analyzed.

Experiments on image and video tasks report speedups of up to 1.4 times for models including DeiT and TimeSformer, with less than 0.7% accuracy sacrificed. The authors also report qualitative and quantitative evidence that the resulting interpretations can outperform raw Transformer attention and off-the-shelf interpretation methods. The findings combine an empirical efficiency benefit with a more understandable account of the model's input selection.
neurips-2021-ia-red-2-interpretability-a.tldr: IA-RED² dynamically removes redundant visual tokens, delivering reported speedups of up to 1.4 times alongside interpretable selection behavior.

paragraphs: Learning to approximate solutions can be useful when many related, computationally difficult optimization problems must be solved repeatedly. Supervised approaches typically use previously solved instances as training examples. This paper examines a difficulty in that strategy: similar problem instances can receive very different solution labels, making the mapping harder for a model to learn.

Such variability can arise when the solver returns approximate answers, when a problem has symmetric solutions, or when the solver uses randomization. The issue is therefore partly how the training targets are produced. The authors connect this volatility in the solution data to the learner's ability to approximate it.

They propose a method for generating exact or approximate solutions that are more amenable to supervised learning. Its effectiveness is tested on difficult nonlinear nonconvex problems and discrete combinatorial problems. The contribution shifts attention toward the preparation of solution examples: improving their learnability is another route to improving learned optimization, alongside changes to the predictive model itself.
neurips-2021-learning-hard-optimization-.tldr: The paper makes optimization-solution training data more learnable by addressing large differences between labels for closely related instances.

paragraphs: This paper investigates one reason neural networks can outperform kernel methods in image classification: their ability to discover a sparse useful signal amid strong noise. The proposed explanation focuses on adapting features to local signal structure, complementing explanations based on the complexity of the functions a network can represent.

For a simple data distribution containing sparse signal and high-variance noise, the authors prove that a simple convolutional network trained with stochastic gradient descent learns to threshold away noise and identify the signal. Its corresponding neural tangent kernel uses predetermined features and cannot adapt in the same way under this analysis.

Experiments with CIFAR-10 and MNIST images placed against different backgrounds illustrate the same phenomenon. As background noise grows stronger, the convolutional network remains relatively robust, while its corresponding neural tangent kernel loses substantial performance. The authors call this local signal adaptivity and present it as one explanation of the performance gap. The theorem concerns the specified simple distribution, while the image experiments provide related empirical evidence.
neurips-2021-local-signal-adaptivity-pro.tldr: Theory and image experiments show how learned convolutional features can isolate sparse signals from noise more effectively than corresponding fixed kernel features.

paragraphs: The paper asks how accurately one can estimate nonlinear summaries of a categorical distribution when individual observations are protected by local differential privacy. The original samples are independent and identically distributed over K categories. Only privatized versions are public, with each version produced from one person's attribute under privacy level alpha.

The target summaries are power sums: add together each category probability raised to a positive power gamma. The authors study how estimation risk depends on the number of categories, sample size, and privacy level. They analyze two non-interactive plug-in estimators, where estimates of the probabilities are used to construct the desired summary, and obtain slower rates under the privacy constraint.

The paper also introduces a sequentially interactive two-step procedure for gamma greater than one. For gamma at least two, it attains the stated parametric rate of one divided by the square root of n alpha squared. Lower bounds cover all permitted local-privacy mechanisms and estimators, helping characterize the fundamental accuracy limits alongside the proposed procedures.
neurips-2021-locally-differentially-priv.tldr: The paper characterizes private estimation of categorical power sums and shows that an interactive procedure attains a parametric rate for powers at least two.

paragraphs: Neural Human Performer aims to render human performance videos from freely chosen viewpoints using sparse multi-camera observations. Generalizing to new people and poses is difficult because body parts move relative to one another and frequently become occluded. The paper addresses these challenges with a generalizable neural radiance field grounded in a parametric human body model.

A temporal transformer aggregates visual features tracked over time using skeletal motion. This connects observations of moving body regions across frames. A second transformer combines the temporally aggregated features with features aligned to image pixels, using cross-attention to integrate the available camera views at each time step.

The approach brings together body structure, temporal evidence, and multiple viewpoints in the representation used for rendering. On ZJU-MoCap and AIST, the authors report significantly better results than recent generalizable NeRF methods for unseen identities and poses. Those evaluations support the value of explicitly organizing observations around human motion when transferring a rendering model beyond the people and poses seen during training.
neurips-2021-neural-human-performer-lear.tldr: Neural Human Performer combines body-guided temporal features and multi-view attention to improve rendering of unseen people and poses.

paragraphs: Training large neural networks across many accelerators involves several interacting choices. Data parallelism distributes data processing, pipeline parallelism divides model stages, and tensor parallelism splits computations within layers. Memory-saving techniques add further options. Piper addresses the difficult planning problem of combining these choices while partitioning the network's computation across the available accelerators.

The proposed optimization algorithm uses two levels of dynamic programming. Its central insight is to start with supplied tensor-parallelization techniques for individual layers. Having these layer-level choices substantially reduces the search space compared with considering tensor-parallel configurations across the entire network operator graph.

This restriction makes the global planning problem tractable within the proposed approach while still combining several parallelism modes and memory optimizations. The contribution is an efficient way to organize a complex optimization problem around useful layer-level building blocks. Its tractability argument depends on those provided techniques, such as established transformer-layer splits, being available as inputs to the planner.
neurips-2021-piper-multidimensional-plan.tldr: Piper uses two-level dynamic programming and supplied layer-level tensor splits to plan combinations of parallelism and memory optimizations.

paragraphs: Planning directly from images requires a system to connect visual perception with reasoning about sequences of actions. The paper focuses on environments where the underlying search problem is combinatorially difficult. Such problems can challenge methods that perform well on other visual control tasks, particularly when those methods must generalize to unfamiliar variations.

The proposed method learns to represent the environment as a latent graph. A key ingredient is state reidentification: recognizing when observations correspond to a state already encountered. By using that recognition, the method reduces the stated complexity of finding a good policy from exponential to linear. The authors also introduce lightweight environments with discrete combinatorial structure and planning challenges difficult even for humans.

Experiments show strong generalization to variations in these environments. The reported settings include one-shot planning and offline reinforcement learning supplied only with low-quality trajectories. These results support the usefulness of learning a reusable graph of states for visual planning, including situations where opportunities to gather high-quality experience are restricted.
neurips-2021-planning-from-pixels-in-env.tldr: Learning a latent state graph and recognizing repeated states reduces the stated planning complexity and supports strong empirical generalization from pixels.

paragraphs: PLUGIn addresses generative inversion: recovering the hidden code that produced an observation through a known neural generator. The observation may contain added noise, so recovering the code can also help reconstruct a cleaner generated output. The proposed algorithm uses partially linearized updates to estimate that code.

For a d-layer ReLU generator with Gaussian weights, the authors prove geometric convergence to a neighborhood of the true code with high probability, provided layer widths satisfy bounds growing roughly as 5 to the layer index times the input width, up to logarithmic factors. These conditions allow some layers to be narrower than their predecessors, extending the guarantee to networks with certain contractive layers.

After sufficiently many iterations, errors in both the latent code and generated output are bounded in order by the noise magnitude times the square root of 4^d n0/nd. Thus, a sufficiently large output-to-input expansion ratio can enable denoising. Synthetic and real-data experiments support the theory and illustrate removal of image artifacts.
neurips-2021-plugin-a-simple-algorithm-f.tldr: PLUGIn recovers latent codes from noisy generator outputs with conditional convergence guarantees that allow some contractive layers.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph embeddings represent entities and relations numerically so that a model can predict missing links. Their usefulness depends partly on whether they capture recurring logical patterns. This paper focuses on transitivity: when a relation from one entity to a second, and from the second to a third, implies the same relation from the first to the third.

The authors first show theoretically that projections can model transitive relations. They then introduce Rot-Pro, which combines projections with relation-specific rotations. This combination is intended to add support for transitivity while retaining the ability to express other important relation patterns within the same embedding model.

The paper proves that Rot-Pro can infer symmetry, asymmetry, inversion, composition, and transitivity. Experiments show that it effectively learns transitive structure and achieves state-of-the-art link prediction on the evaluated datasets containing transitive relations. The theoretical result concerns the model's capacity to capture these patterns, while the experiments demonstrate the practical benefit of that capacity in the stated datasets.
neurips-2021-rot-pro-modeling-transitivi.tldr: Rot-Pro combines projections and rotations to capture transitivity alongside other relation patterns and improve link prediction on datasets containing transitive relations.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression searches for mathematical expressions that explain observed outputs from an unknown process. The candidate expressions form a difficult discrete search space. This paper combines neural-guided search with genetic programming, using the neural component to improve where the evolutionary search starts rather than tightly directing every stage of its progress.

The neural component seeds the initial population for a random-restart genetic programming procedure and gradually learns to propose better starting populations. Genetic programming then runs for many generations. The authors find that allowing these generations to proceed without interdependence on the neural component works better for symbolic regression than more strongly coupled alternatives.

On common expression-recovery benchmarks, the hybrid recovers 65% more expressions than a recently published top-performing model under the same experimental setup. The paper also introduces 22 harder symbolic regression benchmark problems. The findings support a division of work in which learned guidance supplies promising initial candidates and evolutionary search develops them through extended independent exploration.
neurips-2021-symbolic-regression-via-dee.tldr: A neural model learns better starting populations for genetic programming, increasing expression recovery by 65% in the reported benchmark comparison.

paragraphs: The paper studies point forecasting for a single time series, where the goal is to predict future values from historical observations. It asks whether local topological structure can provide useful information alongside the raw measurements. Persistent homology supplies these topological features, giving the forecasting model another description of patterns in its recent history.

The proposed topological attention mechanism lets a model attend to local topological features within a historical time window. It can be integrated into existing forecasting architectures and trained end to end. This makes topology an additional signal that the forecasting system can use selectively as part of its prediction process.

Combined with N-BEATS, the approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on M4, a benchmark containing 100,000 diverse time series. Ablation experiments and comparisons in a setting with only one time series available for training also support the benefit of including these features through attention. The evidence therefore links the added structural information to improved forecasts in several evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-topological-attention-for-t.tldr: Topological attention adds local persistent-homology features to forecasting models and achieves state-of-the-art M4 results when combined with N-BEATS.
